To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mapping tori of exponentially growing automorphisms of free groups are strongly relatively hyperbolic, that the acylindrical accessibility of the mapping tori implies their strong relative hyperbolicity and, that the mapping torii of exponentially growing automorphism are acylindrically accessible.

free-by-cyclic groups with an exponentially growing automorphism are strongly relatively hyperbolic, that free-by-free groups with an exponential isoperimetric function are hyperbolic relative to a single cyclic subgroup, and that free-by-free hyperbolics have an isoperimetric quadratic function.
free-by-cyclic groups are strongly relatively hyperbolic, acylindrically hyperbolic and satisfy the quadratic isoperimetry inequality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the geometry of free-by-cubic extensions, which is a natural generalization of the geometry of free groups and free-by-free groups.
the study of the dynamics of free group automorphisms and their mapping tori.
the study of the geometric properties of the mapping torus $M_\phi$ of a group endomorphism $\phi$ of a finitely generated group $\mathbb G$, where $\phi$ is an exponentially growing map.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a free-by-cyclic group is relatively hyperbolic (with a strong relative hyperbolicity constant) whenever it contains an exponentially growing automorphism.
the free-by-cyclic groups are the most general class of groups which can be hyperbolic.
a group $\mathsf{F}\times_{\phi}\mathbb{Z}$ is (strongly/acyclindrically) hyperbolic if and only if $\phi$ grows exponentially fast.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the geometry of free-by-cyclical groups is very similar to the geometry of hyperbolic groups.
the free-by-cyclic group is a natural generalization of the hyperbolic group.
the mapping tori of $\mathbb{Z}$-actions on hyperbolic groups are (strongly) hyperbolic, and the mapping tori on free-by-cyclic groups are (strong) relative hyperbolic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use a combination of geometric group theory techniques to answer questions in low-dimensional topology. [1]
the study of relative hyperbolicity in free-by-cyclic groups is intimately connected to the study of free-by-free groups.
, for free-by-cyclic groups, the geometry of the mapping torus is closely related to the geometry of the base group $\mathbb F$.
